summary: Introduces the IOAM Direct Export (DEX) option type for in situ OAM. Rather than carrying telemetry data inside packets, the option triggers the data to be exported directly from network nodes for collection. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: In situ OAM works by adding small pieces of measurement data to packets while they travel, so a collector can trace the path they took. This RFC adds a different mode: a flag in the packet that tells every node on the path to send its measurements off separately, instead of carrying them onwards.

questions: how does ioam export telemetry data
what is the ioam dex option type
how does dex avoid overloading collectors
what is the flow id in ioam dex
subtitle: A trigger option that tells IOAM nodes to export or collect telemetry on the spot, instead of stuffing it into the packet.

tldr.problem: In situ OAM normally pushes telemetry data into packets as they travel, which makes packets grow along the path. Operators sometimes want the data to leave the packet right away instead.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9326 defines the IOAM Direct Export (DEX) Option-Type. An encapsulating node adds it to selected packets, and the nodes that see it collect and export the requested IOAM data without writing it into the packet.
tldr.outcome: Direct export adds a trigger that can cause every node on a path to emit data, so the RFC requires selective use and rate limiting to avoid overloading the network or the receiving entity.

facts.label: Recommended rate limit
facts.value: 1/N of interface capacity, N greater than 100

today: RFC 9326 is a Proposed Standard, published in November 2022. No RFC obsoletes it and no RFC updates it. It builds on RFC 9197, which defines the other IOAM option types.

sections.title: Exporting Telemetry Instead of Carrying It
sections.content:
IOAM (RFC 9197) is used for monitoring traffic in the network and for incorporating IOAM data fields into in-flight data packets. IOAM makes use of four possible IOAM-Option-Types defined in RFC 9197: Pre-allocated Trace, Incremental Trace, Proof of Transit and Edge-to-Edge.

This document defines a new IOAM-Option-Type called the IOAM Direct Export (DEX) Option-Type. It is used as a trigger for IOAM nodes to locally aggregate and process IOAM data and, or, to export it to a receiving entity or entities. The RFC calls this functionality collection and exporting. A receiving entity is an entity that resides within the IOAM domain, such as a collector, an analyzer, a controller, a decapsulating node, or a software module in one of the IOAM nodes.

Even though the Option-Type is called Direct Export, it depends on the deployment whether the receipt of a packet with a DEX Option-Type leads to the creation of another packet. Some deployments might simply use the packet with the DEX Option-Type to trigger local processing of operations, administration and maintenance data, and the functionality of that local processing is not within the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally an IOAM option is a container that each node on the path fills in as the packet goes by. The DEX option is different: it does not carry anything itself. It is a marker that says which data fields the nodes should collect, and the nodes send that data out on their own.

sections.title: Where the DEX Option-Type Acts
sections.content:
The DEX Option-Type is used as a trigger for collecting IOAM data locally or exporting it to a receiving entity or entities. It can be used as a trigger for collecting IOAM data by an IOAM node and locally aggregating it, so that this aggregated data can be periodically pushed to a receiving entity or pulled by a receiving entity on demand.

The Option-Type is incorporated into data packets by an IOAM encapsulating node and removed by an IOAM decapsulating node. It can be read, but not modified, by transit nodes. The trigger applies to transit nodes, the decapsulating node and the encapsulating node. An encapsulating node configured to incorporate the DEX Option-Type encapsulates the packets, or possibly a subset of the packets, it forwards with it, and may export and collect the requested IOAM data immediately. Only IOAM encapsulating nodes are allowed to add the DEX Option-Type to a packet. An encapsulating node can also generate probe packets that incorporate the Option-Type, periodically or on demand, for example triggered by the management plane; the specification of such probe packets is outside the scope of the document. A transit node that processes a packet with the DEX Option-Type may export and collect the requested IOAM data. A decapsulating node that processes such a packet may export and collect the requested data and MUST decapsulate the IOAM header.

As in RFC 9197, the DEX Option-Type can be incorporated into all or a subset of the traffic forwarded by the encapsulating node, and the IOAM nodes respond to the DEX trigger by exporting and collecting IOAM data either for all traversing packets that carry the Option-Type or selectively only for a subset of them.
sections.plainLanguage: The node that starts a flow puts the marker in the packet. Every node it passes through may then send its own measurements off to a collector. The node that ends the flow takes the marker out again, and the packet continues without it.

sections.title: The DEX Option-Type Format
sections.content:
The length of the DEX Option-Type is at least 8 octets. It may include one or more optional fields, and the existence of an optional field is indicated by the corresponding flag in the Extension-Flags field. Two optional fields are defined: the Flow ID and the Sequence Number. Every optional field MUST be exactly 4 octets long, so the Extension-Flags field explicitly indicates the length of the option. Defining a new optional field requires an allocation of a corresponding flag in the Extension-Flags field.

The first field is the Namespace-ID, a 16-bit identifier of the IOAM namespace as defined in RFC 9197. Next comes the Flags field, an 8-bit field made of eight 1-bit subfields, and the Extension-Flags field, also 8 bits made of eight 1-bit subfields. Every bit in the Extension-Flags field that is set to 1 indicates the existence of a corresponding optional 4-octet field, and an IOAM node that receives a DEX Option-Type with an unknown flag set to 1 MUST ignore the corresponding optional field. The IOAM-Trace-Type is a 24-bit identifier that specifies which IOAM-Data-Fields should be exported, in the format defined in RFC 9197. Specifically, the bit that corresponds to the Checksum Complement IOAM-Data-Field SHOULD be assigned to be zero by the encapsulating node and ignored by transit and decapsulating nodes, because the Checksum Complement is intended for in-flight packet modifications and is not relevant for direct exporting. The Reserved field MUST be ignored by the receiver.

The optional fields, if present, reside after the Reserved field, in the order of the bits enabled in the Extension-Flags field, starting from the most significant bit. The Flow ID is an optional 32-bit field representing the flow identifier. If the actual Flow ID is shorter than 32 bits it is zero padded in its most significant bits. The field is set at the encapsulating node, and it can be used to correlate the exported data of the same flow from multiple nodes and from multiple packets. Flow ID values are expected to be allocated so that they do not collide: random assignment can be subject to collisions, while centralized allocation avoids the problem, and the specification of the allocation method is outside the scope of the document. The Sequence Number is an optional 32-bit number starting from 0 and incremented by 1 for each packet from the same flow at the encapsulating node that includes the DEX option. Combined with the Flow ID, it gives a convenient way to correlate the exported data from the same user packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is at least eight bytes long and has room for two extra four-byte fields. The first says which flow the packet belongs to, so the collector can group the measurements from different nodes together. The second counts the packets in that flow, so the collector can tell them apart.

sections.title: Sampling and Rate Limiting
sections.content:
If an IOAM encapsulating node incorporates the DEX Option-Type into all the traffic it forwards, it may lead to an excessive amount of exported data, which may overload the network and the receiving entity. An encapsulating node that supports the DEX Option-Type MUST therefore be able to incorporate it selectively into a subset of the packets it forwards. Various methods of packet selection and sampling have been defined previously, in RFC 7014 and RFC 5475, and similar techniques can be applied to select the subset of forwarded traffic.

The subset of traffic forwarded or transmitted with a DEX Option-Type SHOULD NOT exceed 1/N of the interface capacity on any of the encapsulating node's interfaces, counting both forwarded traffic and generated probe packets. N is a parameter that network operators can configure. If there is an upper bound M on the number of IOAM transit nodes on any path in the network, it is RECOMMENDED to use an N much greater than M, because a packet carrying a DEX Option-Type may trigger an exported packet from each transit node along the path, for a total of M exported packets. If there is no prior knowledge about the network topology or size, it is RECOMMENDED to use N greater than 100.

An IOAM node that performs DEX-triggered exporting MUST support the ability to limit the rate of the exported packets. That rate SHOULD be limited so that the number of exported packets is significantly lower than the number of packets forwarded by the device, and the exported data rate SHOULD NOT exceed 1/N of the interface capacity on any of the node's interfaces, again with N greater than 100 recommended. Depending on the node's architecture, the export rate may be limited to a lower number to avoid loading the node. A node may keep a counter of the events in which it received a packet with the DEX Option-Type and did not collect or export data because of the rate limits.

IOAM nodes SHOULD NOT be configured to export packets over a path or a tunnel that is itself subject to IOAM direct exporting, and encapsulating nodes that can identify a packet as an IOAM exported packet MUST NOT push a DEX Option-Type into such a packet. This is intended to prevent nested exporting and exporting loops. A transit or decapsulating node that receives an unknown IOAM-Option-Type ignores it, so nodes that do not support the DEX Option-Type ignore it. A decapsulating node removes the IOAM encapsulation and all its IOAM-Option-Types, which applies when one of those options is a possibly unknown DEX Option-Type.
sections.plainLanguage: Two limits keep this from becoming a flood. The encapsulating node marks only a small fraction of its traffic, so only that fraction triggers exports. Each node that exports then caps how many export packets it sends. The recommendation of N greater than 100 exists because every node on the path may export, so one marked packet can turn into several exported packets.

sections.title: Performance Considerations
sections.content:
The DEX Option-Type triggers IOAM data to be collected and exported packets to be sent to a receiving entity or entities. In some cases this may impact the receiving entity's performance or the performance along the paths leading to it.

The performance impact of these exported packets is limited by taking two measures: selective DEX encapsulation at the encapsulating nodes, and limiting the exporting rate at the transit nodes. These two measures ensure that direct exporting is used at a rate that does not significantly affect the network bandwidth and does not overload the receiving entity. Moreover, it is possible to load balance the exported data among multiple receiving entities, although the exporting method is not within the scope of the document.

It should be noted that in some networks, DEX data may be exported over an out-of-band network in which a large volume of exported traffic does not compromise user traffic. In this case, an operator may choose to disable the exporting rate limiting.
sections.plainLanguage: Exporting costs bandwidth and work at the collector. The sampling and rate limits keep that cost small. If the exports travel on a separate management network, the operator can turn the rate limit off.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of IOAM in general are discussed in RFC 9197. Specifically, an attacker may try to use the functionality defined here to attack the network. An attacker may attempt to overload network devices by injecting synthetic packets that include the DEX Option-Type. Similarly, an on-path attacker may maliciously incorporate the DEX Option-Type into transit packets, or maliciously remove it from packets in which it is incorporated.

Forcing DEX, either in synthetic packets or in transit packets, may overload the IOAM nodes and the receiving entities. Since the mechanism affects multiple devices along the network path, it potentially amplifies the effect on the network bandwidth, on the storage of the devices that collect the data, and on the receiving entity's load. The amplification may be worse in wide area networks with multiple IOAM domains. If DEX is used in one IOAM domain to export data to a receiving entity, the exported packets can be forwarded through a second domain, where they are themselves subject to DEX, and the exported packets of the second domain may be forwarded through yet another. Theoretically this recursive amplification could continue indefinitely.

Three requirements mitigate these attacks. Selective DEX is applied by encapsulating nodes to limit the potential impact to a small fraction of the traffic. Rate limiting of exported traffic is applied by IOAM nodes to prevent overloading attacks and to significantly limit the scale of amplification attacks. And encapsulating nodes are required to avoid pushing the DEX Option-Type into IOAM exported packets, which prevents some of the amplification and export loop scenarios.

Although the exporting method is out of scope, any exporting method MUST secure the exported data from the IOAM node to the receiving entity, to protect its confidentiality and guarantee its integrity. An IOAM node that performs DEX exporting MUST send the exported data to a pre-configured trusted receiving entity in the same IOAM domain, and MUST gain explicit consent to export data to a receiving entity before starting to send exported data. An attacker may keep track of the information sent in DEX headers as a means of reconnaissance, which can be mitigated to some extent by careful allocation of the Flow ID and Sequence Number space so that it does not compromise privacy aspects such as customer identities. The integrity of the DEX Option-Type can be protected through the encapsulating protocol, but the integrity protection mechanism for IOAM-Data-Fields does not apply, because the DEX Option-Type does not include IOAM-Data-Fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The danger is amplification: one marked packet can cause every node on the path to send a packet of its own, and an attacker could inject marked packets deliberately. The sampling rule, the rate limit and the ban on marking exported packets all exist to stop that.
